newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - Planemakers blitz Hungary in pre-NATO hard sell.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Planemakers blitz Hungary in pre-NATO hard sell.

text.p: Hungarian test pilot Zsolt Racz has been doing a lot of flying in what could be his most important mission ever, to help his country decide which fighters will serve its needs into the 21st century.

The world's biggest planemakers are lining up for an anticipated deal to sell Hungary $1 billion worth of fighters to replace its ageing fleet of 30 Soviet MiG-21s and MiG-23s which fly alongside the country's 28 more modern MiG 29s.
The tender had been due for publication last summer but Hungary postponed it until after a decision by NATO on expansion, expected at the alliance's Madrid summit next month.

Of the three countries most expected to be invited to join, -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- Hungary is the most advanced in its preparations to upgrade its air force and could set an important precedent, with Poland notably in the market for up to 100 multi-purpose fighters.

A Saab /British Aerospace Plc consortium is offering the JAS 39 Gripen while U.S. giants Lockheed Martin Corp and McDonnell Douglas Corp, with the F16/C and F18 Hornet, and France's Dassault Aviation, with the Mirage 2000-5, are also in the race. Russia is reported to be considering offering MiG 29s and SU 39s.
As part of the four Western companies' hard sell, Lieutenant-Colonel Racz, a MiG 29 specialist, has been asked to fly all but the Gripen, which he is due to try out this month.
"There are differences," he told Reuters. "The F18 is better on slow speed and high angle of attack, the F16 is has a very strong thrust/weight ratio. All of them will do the job."

Although Racz won't admit it, the pilots' favourite seems to be the twin-engined, but expensive F18. "The MiG 29 has two engines and I now understand how important that can be, we could have lost the aircraft if we hadn't had two engines."
HUNGARY LOOKING FOR ECONOMIC PAYOFF
But whatever Racz thinks, the technical specifications of the aircraft are unlikely to be the deciding factor.
The Hungarian government has made it clear that industrial packages attached to the deal which stimulate Hungarian jobs and exports will be very important in assessing the bids.
"If you look at the procurement documents...there's a very strong hint that Hungary wants a lot out of this but not just in military terms," says Paul Beaver, of Jane's Defence Weekly.
And, Beaver says, Saab's parent company, the Wallenberg group, is well ahead of the pack in that regard.
"The Swedes have been very clever at saying 'Well, how else can we help the Hungarian economy, how can we give added value to our bid?' and they've done this with a lot of their plans."

The Wallenberg group was the first to sign an industrial offset deal with the Hungarian government in September 1995 and last month another Wallenberg company, AB Electrolux, announced it would invest $35 million in the Hungarian Lehel freezer plant it acquired in 1991.

Electrolux says this takes its total direct investment in Hungary usable as offset against the Gripen to around $100 million. Lockheed, McDonnell Douglas and engine maker General Electric Co are only beginning to enact industrial packages signed this year while Dassault has yet to initial a deal.
"We believe our industrial back-up is our biggest asset," said Jan Narlinge, Gripen/British Aerospace consortium vice-president for Industrial Cooperation.
However, Saab's industrial packages may be premature, say its competitors.

Lockheed International vice-president Doug Miller said his company would announce concrete proposals only after the tender details are made public but added Lockheed was already exploring high-tech and infrastructure as areas of development.
"We'll focus on increasing exports and increasing the current technology level...we're very interested in improving the overall competitiveness of the country," he told Reuters.

Dassault maintains it should be taken just as seriously as the other potential Western bidders despite being the only one with neither an offset deal with the Hungarian government nor an office in Budapest. It says it will sign an offset arrangement "within one or two months".

"Sometimes the Hungarians say, 'Maybe you are late for the offset programme'," Dassault's European military sales manager Serge Rigaux told Reuters. "We don't go so fast because we think we have to go in our way, step by step."
But the Gripen consortium denies it may have peaked early.

"The key is that we can direct our efforts if we have a solid base in this country," said Hans Kruger, Gripen's senior vice president. "If we find that we're not successful in the fighter business then we can direct the business other ways."
Kruger's talk of losing the contract may betray the fear that the JAS 39's strength -- it's the newest of the four Western designs -- could also be its weakness.

While Lockheed boasts almost 1000 F16s in service with NATO in Europe, the Gripen is used only by Denmark, prompting Lockheed to dub the F16, "NATO's standard fighter", much to the annoyance of Dassault's Rigaux.
"It's crazy to call it the NATO standard. Our aircraft is perfectly interoperable with the NATO forces -- every day we are working with them," Rigaux said.
US GOVERNMENT PLAYS THE SECOND HAND CARD
But both Kruger and Rigaux may also be worried about what looks like a trump card from the U.S. government -- the offer of cut-price used F16s or F18s from its air force or navy.
"For a five year period a limited number of aircraft could be leased by Hungary at much lower cost than if they were to be new," a Budapest U.S. Embassy source told Reuters.
"This would allow Hungary to develop a lot of the support infrastructure necessary...and it will facilitate a purchase later on if they want to continue with the same aircraft."
The deal could result in Hungary getting 28 F16/A fighters and back-up for under half the $1 billion cost of new planes.
Hungary's defence ministry, which says it needs a 65 percent increase in the military budget next year, sees the offer's attraction.
"Certainly, given the economic difficulties we have to face in the future for me this a very tempting possibility," said Istvan Gyarmati, a defence ministry official for NATO integration.
Even Gripen's Narlinge recognises it could be an offer the Hungarians cannot refuse.

"Politicians have to be re-elected within a time frame that means they can't be as long-term as industrialists," he said. "If you have a problem you have to solve in the short term and you don't have enough money you may go for second best."

A fact of which Lt Col Racz is all too aware as Narlinge plays host to him this week. Racz realises his evaluation will be far from decisive but as Lockheed's own F16 chief test pilot Steve Barter notes, Gripen should still pull out the stops.
"Zsolt is far from having the final say, but one thing's for sure -- if he doesn't like the plane, the deal's dead."
